original_question: Is every compact embedded surface in R^3 with constant mean curvature and circular boundary necessarily either a planar disk or a spherical cap?
target_in_paper: Conjecture 1 in Section 1 (Introduction), restated as Problem 2.1 in Section 2 (Part I: circular boundary).
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the paper’s intended problem almost exactly: the ambient space is Euclidean 3-space, the surface is compact and embedded, the mean curvature is constant, the boundary is a circle, and the proposed rigidity conclusion is precisely ‘planar disk or spherical cap.’
missing_details: The paper’s official formulation is for a surface spanning a single round circle S^1, not just vaguely having a ‘circular boundary.’
Section 1 fixes the convention that ‘having C as boundary’ means the boundary map Ψ|∂Σ: ∂Σ → C is a diffeomorphism, so the entire boundary is exactly that one circle.
To be fully stand-alone and paper-faithful, it is better to say ‘constant mean curvature surface in R^3 whose boundary is exactly a round circle S^1.’
The conclusion should be understood as the planar disk bounded by that same circle or a spherical cap bounded by that same circle.
The nearby discussion shows that the intended sharp reformulation is via the plane P containing the circle: the hard point is whether such a surface can have points on both sides of P.
refined_question: Let Ψ: Σ → R^3 be a compact embedded surface of constant mean curvature whose boundary is exactly one round circle S^1 (that is, Ψ|∂Σ: ∂Σ → S^1 is a diffeomorphism). Must Ψ(Σ) be either the planar disk bounded by S^1 or a spherical cap bounded by S^1?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, is every compact embedded constant-mean-curvature surface in R^3 spanning a round circle S^1 forced to lie entirely in one of the closed half-spaces determined by the plane P containing S^1? The paper explains that once this one-sidedness is known, Alexandrov reflection gives the desired classification.
justification: The nearest official statement is the introduction’s Conjecture 1, which says that planar disks and spherical caps are the only compact embedded cmc surfaces in R^3 with circular boundary. Section 2 then repeats the same question as Problem 2.1 in the sharper form ‘spanning a circle.’ The notation immediately before Section 2 clarifies what it means for a surface to have a closed curve C as boundary, so that point should be made explicit in a stand-alone rewrite. The discussion following Problem 2.1 shows the paper’s intended reduction: if the surface lies on one side of the boundary plane P, Alexandrov reflection forces rotational symmetry and hence the standard examples; therefore the real unresolved issue is whether an embedded cmc surface spanning a circle can cross the boundary plane. In the available arXiv/PDF version, the labels are Conjecture 1 and Problem 2.1 rather than Conjecture 1.1.

citations.label: Notation: 'Σ has C as a boundary'
